newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: China fall-out could cost Dutch business billions.
newsitem.headline: China fall-out could cost Dutch business billions.

text.p: Dutch companies stand to lose up to two billion guilders' worth of contracts now that a government-led trade mission to China has been postponed indefinitely, industry lobby VNO/NCW said on Wednesday.
"Dutch companies may very well have missed out on 1.5 to 2.0 billion guilders worth of turnover over the next three to four years," VNO/NCW spokesman Elmar Bouma said.
The Dutch government said on Tuesday Peking had postponed the mission, scheduled for June 7 to 14, because of the Netherlands' support for a U.N. resolution critical of China's human rights record.

"Contracts totalling some 700 million guilders were ready to be signed," Bouma said, adding "experience has shown that done deals generate as much (turnover) again in the way of follow-up orders and spin-offs over three to four years."
Now that the trade mission had been postponed it was questionable whether the orders already agreed would be signed, and if so when, Bouma said.
Bouma declined to name the Dutch companies in question, but said the contracts were for projects in the infrastructure, general construction and environment sectors.

The Netherlands, with Denmark, the United States and 12 other countries, is co-sponsoring a resolution criticising China's human rights record. China has warned that relations with these countries will be affected.

"This Chinese step must be linked to the role that the Netherlands...has played in drawing attention to human rights in China at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva," the ministry of economic affairs said on Tuesday.

The mission, led by economic affairs minister Hans Wijers, was to have included 47 companies active in infrastructure, financial services, the agro-industry, transport, chemicals and food wholesaling and retailing.
VNO/NCW chief Hans Blankert said the Dutch action had shown a lack of understanding of China's sensitivity to public criticism of its policies.
"We (the Netherlands) have fallen on our faces a couple of times now and I hope to consult with the ministers concerned how this may be avoided in future," Blankert said.
"It is rather odd that the Netherlands first spends a number of years carefully building up relations with China only to raise a highly sensitive issue like this at the moment supreme," Bouma added.
